To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

rhesus monkeys prefer the larger of two intravenous doses of cocaine, and they obtain almost all of their drug reinforcers under conditions in which the dose on one of two levers is systematically varied within a large range.
concurrent performances were always controlled by the larger of the two doses of cocaine and that, under our conditions, exclusive preferences were obtained for all dose combinations tested.
concurrent performances are sensitive to dose of intravenous cocaine, with the larger doses being more reinforcing than the smaller doses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the amount of drug obtained and the rate of responding under a variety of experimental conditions.

the development of a procedure that will permit the assessment of the effects of cocaine on the behavior of animals and humans, and the effects of behavior on the pharmacokinetics of cocaine in animals and humans.
the development of procedures for assessing the effects of different drugs on the behavior of monkeys.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the dose of cocaine that was available on the variable-doser lever was the major determinant of preference for cocaine.
the dose of cocaine that was preferred was the dose that was most effective.
the dose of cocaine was an important factor in the concurrent performances, but that the relative dose differences between levers were the most important factor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the relative effectiveness of different doses of cocaine is a function of the dose of cocaine that the subject has been exposed to previously, and that this function may be described as a monotonic increase in the relative effectiveness of cocaine with increasing dose.

the relative reinforcing effects of different doses of cocaine were reflected in relative response rates and that, under the conditions of our experiments, these relative rates of responding were a function of drug dose.
the dose of cocaine that is preferred is that which maximizes the rate of drug self-administration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dose-effect function for cocaine is not linear.
concurrent procedures are a powerful tool for studying the effects of drugs on choice behavior.
concurrent procedures, in which the reinforcers differ only in dose, are a good way to measure preference for different doses of a drug.
